items.stem: What is the difference between a criterion and a constraint?

options.text: A criterion is a goal the design aims for; a constraint is a limit it must stay within
A criterion is a limit; a constraint is a goal
They mean exactly the same thing
A criterion applies only to cars and a constraint only to bikes

items.explanation: Criteria are the goals you want, like speed or low cost. Constraints are the fixed limits you must respect, like a budget or the materials available.

items.stem: A design team is told the product must weigh under 2 kilograms. This requirement is a

options.text: criterion
tradeoff
constraint
prototype

items.explanation: A fixed limit the design must stay within is a constraint. A maximum weight the design cannot exceed is a boundary, not a goal.

items.stem: An engineer makes a drone's frame thinner to reduce its weight, but now the frame bends more easily. This is an example of a

options.text: constraint
tradeoff
criterion
decision matrix

items.explanation: Gaining one quality (less weight) by giving up another (strength) is a tradeoff. Improving one criterion often worsens another.

items.stem: Why is it usually impossible to make a design that is best at every criterion at once?

options.text: Engineers are not skilled enough to do it
The criteria often trade against each other, so improving one worsens another
There are never enough materials
Customers do not want good designs

items.explanation: Criteria pull against each other. Making a product faster, cheaper, lighter, and stronger all at once is rarely possible, so engineers must balance them.

items.stem: What does it mean to optimize a design?

options.text: To make it perfect at every single criterion
To remove all of its constraints
To adjust it so it meets the most important criteria as well as possible within the constraints
To copy a competing design exactly

items.explanation: Optimization is finding the best balance for the important criteria while staying inside the constraints. It manages tradeoffs rather than erasing them.

items.stem: A team compares three designs by scoring each one on speed, cost, and safety, then adding the scores. What tool are they using?

options.text: a prototype
a constraint list
a decision matrix
a boundary

items.explanation: A decision matrix scores each competing design against the criteria so the options can be compared fairly, side by side.

items.stem: In a decision matrix, what does weighting do?

options.text: It gives the most important criteria extra value in the total
It makes every design score the same
It removes the lowest-scoring design automatically
It measures how heavy each design is

items.explanation: Weighting gives more importance to the criteria that matter most, so those rows count for more when the scores are added up.

items.stem: Two phones solve the same need in different ways: one has a huge battery and one is very thin and light. These are best described as

options.text: constraints
competing solutions
prototypes of each other
the same design

items.explanation: Competing solutions are two or more different designs for the same problem. Engineers compare them to choose the best fit.

items.stem: In the bike decision matrix, the Cruiser and All-Terrain tied. What is the best way to break the tie?

options.text: Pick the one that looks nicer
Decide which criteria matter most for the rider and weight them
Always choose the cheapest option
Add a brand-new design instead

items.explanation: The best choice depends on the goal. Deciding which criteria matter most and weighting them shows which design fits that particular rider best.

items.stem: Which statement best sums up engineering design?

options.text: Every good design is perfect at everything
The best design has no constraints
Every design involves tradeoffs, and the best one balances them for the goal
Tradeoffs only happen in cheap products

items.explanation: Every real design is a compromise. Because criteria trade against each other within constraints, the best design balances those tradeoffs to fit the goal.
